memory_candidates.content: When a repository-owned script must serialize its own `lake build` (or similar) calls against a build guard that lives in a disposable, regenerated deploy tree (.claude/), take an flock() on the SAME lock path the guard publishes in its own header as a stable convention, rather than probing for or calling the guard binary. Advisory locks are keyed on the filesystem path, not the process that opened them, so the script and the guard exclude each other with zero coupling: no detection logic, no hardcoded reference into the deploy tree, unchanged behavior in a clone with no agent system deployed. A further useful trick: if the lock's file descriptor is opened early and deliberately never explicitly released (no `flock -u`), it stays held until the script process exits, so every LATER .lake-reading step in the same script run inherits the same protection for free, with no additional lock code -- provided those later steps are gated by the same precondition (e.g. the same RUN_BUILD flag) as the first locked step, which should be confirmed by grepping every build-launching call site in the file rather than assumed.

Never run a bare `git stash` (or `git stash pop`) on a shared working tree while concurrent sibling agents are dispatched against it in the same /orchestrate cycle -- and selective post-hoc extraction of only your own declared files is NOT sufficient recovery if you do. Measured incident: a bare `git stash` stashed the entire tree (including siblings' uncommitted work), and the subsequent `git stash pop` conflicted on a sibling's fresh edit and aborted, leaving everything -- including the append-only `specs/events.jsonl` telemetry log -- reverted to its pre-stash HEAD state. Recovering the acting agent's own 3 declared files via `git show stash@{N}:<path> > <path>` looked like a complete recovery (git status showed no sibling *source* file touched), but it silently missed that `events.jsonl` -- a shared, unowned, append-only file nobody's file_scope names and which never conflicts on pop because appends don't collide -- had also been silently reverted, losing 32 rows of real telemetry (lifecycle_stage/session_stop events from two sessions) until a teammate noticed the row-count regression, diffed stash@{N} against HEAD, and merged the union deduped by event_id. The generalizable danger: unowned, no-conflict, append-only files are the EASIEST class to lose in a stash mishap, precisely because nothing about them signals damage (no merge conflict, no diff in your own declared scope) -- 'my files came back fine' is not evidence the tree is intact. The only reliable fix is to never bare-stash a shared tree in the first place: use a read-only `git show HEAD:<path>` or `git diff <path>` to inspect a single file's baseline instead of stashing anything.
